L36: Uniforms are the antithesis of high fashion. Where uniform design focuses on notions of functionality, control, and tradition, fashion promotes constant change, creativity, and subversion. Yet fashion has often drawn inspiration from uniforms of all kinds, taking functional features and transforming them into decorative elements.
L37: Simultaneously designed to blend in and stand out, uniforms occupy a unique place in our society. We encounter uniforms everywhere, from those of soldiers and school children, to the distinctive attire of flight attendants and fast-food clerks. Likewise, the uniforms of athletes and police officers have become familiar, everyday sights. They are overt symbols of social order, but they are also considered so commonplace that they are often overlooked.
L38: Uniformity explores the dynamic history behind a variety of uniforms, considering both their social role and their influence on high fashion. The exhibition is organized thematically to focus on four categories of uniforms: military, work, school, and sports. Uniformity includes over 70 objects from The Museum at FIT’s permanent collection, many of which have never been on view before.

L41: # Army
L42: 
L43: Military uniforms convey their wearers’ nation, rank, regiment, and branch of the armed forces. They help ensure that soldiers immediately recognize a superior officer—as well as enemy troops (or friendly forces) in the field.

L57: The “Ike,” or “Eisenhower,” jacket was added to regulation U.S. Army uniforms during World War II. L67: The U.S. Army issued its first khaki-colored uniforms during the Spanish-American War of 1898 to help camouflage soldiers fighting guerrilla forces. By World War I, brownish- green, wool uniforms (dubbed “olive drabs”) were standard. Most troops hated the color and openly complained about it until the 1950s when it was replaced with a cooler, greyish green.

L71: # Why are so many novels set at Harvard?
L72: 
L73: 【33†Image: Beth Blum.】
L74: 
L75: Photos by Stephanie Mitchell/Harvard Staff Photographer
L76: 
L77: Eileen O’Grady
L78: 
L79: Harvard Staff Writer
L80: 
L81: January 31, 2025 7 min read
L82: ## Beth Blum notes campus is beautiful, romantic setting that lends itself to exploring collision of ideals, reality
L83: In the 2022 novel “Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow” by Gabrielle Zevin ’00, Sam Masur pitches a business proposal to his friend Sadie at the 【34†Harvard Museum of Natural History†www.hmnh.harvard.edu】. “Everything I Never Told You” (2014) by Celeste Ng ’02 uses the 【35†River Houses†dso.college.harvard.edu】 near the John Weeks Footbridge to set a graduate-student love interest.
L84: And Selin Karadağ from “The Idiot” (2017) by Elif Batuman ’99 meets up with senior crush Ivan on the 【36†Widener Library†library.harvard.edu】 steps.
L85: Harvard’s campus has long served as the setting for narrative works by alumni as well as many others.
L86: 【37†Beth Blum, Harris K. Weston Associate Professor of the Humanities†english.fas.harvard.edu】, teaches an 【38†English Department†english.fas.harvard.edu】 【39†course】 that explores books, films, television episodes, and even comics that engage with Harvard as object of cultural intrigue and critique.
L87: In her course, students discuss themes of belonging, tradition, privilege, and competition, research authors’ personal histories in the 【40†Archives†library.harvard.edu】, and even experiment with writing their own Harvard narratives.
L88: In this edited conversation with the Gazette, Blum discusses the longstanding appeal of the genre, for both writers and readers.
L89: 
L90: * * *
L91: 
L92: What counts as a “Harvard Novel”? How do you define the genre?
L93: I see the Harvard novel as a subset of campus fiction, which is simply any fiction set on a college campus — a classic example would perhaps be “Lucky Jim” by Kingsley Amis from 1954.
L94: These books are often either concerned with the tribulations of a professor who is up against a heartless administration, facing their own personal challenges and interpersonal dramas, or with the perspective of a student entering this new world and having to adjust to the realities of a very intense microcosm of the university.
L95: Some stories are explicitly about Harvard and firmly set in the Yard, like Erich Segal’s 1970 hit “Love Story.” Zadie Smith’s “On Beauty,” which she wrote while at 【41†Radcliffe†www.radcliffe.harvard.edu】, is set at the fictional “Wellington College,” a place which shares some traits with Harvard but combines these aspects with those of an imaginary New England liberal arts college environment.
L96: Sometimes Harvard is simply part of a character’s formative backstory, as in “Everything I Never Told You” or “Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow.”
L97: What are some common themes you see across these types of novels?
L98: 
L99: One point that quickly comes across is that attending Harvard is often a family affair. It is entwined with parental expectations and sacrifices, but also with sibling dynamics. This is something we see in “Everything I Never Told You.”
L100: Another prominent theme is student-teacher relationships and the experience of pedagogical projection or transference. In [the 1973 film] “The Paper Chase,” the protagonist, Hart, becomes increasingly obsessed with pleasing his domineering law professor, only to realize at the end that the professor barely knows who he is.
L101: The “street-smart outsider underdog” versus “privileged Harvard insider” is another common trope. This is connected to the contrast between creative idealism and institutional assimilation.
L102: 
L103: Harvard novels can often become a sort of morality tale, where the protagonist learns to embrace their internal values over those imposed by the structures of academic competition.
L104: Belonging is another tremendously prominent motif. The value of community, of the interesting people one meets here, becomes a focal point of the literature.
L105: 
L106: To what do you attribute the longstanding appeal of Harvard’s campus?
L107: 
L108: As my students have pointed out, the University is itself an object of beauty and history. But that romantic history can feel incongruous with the gritty realities of daily living, and the best Harvard stories bring this to the fore.
